title: Two-sided distributive unification with a unit
formal: Let \(E\) be exactly the four identities \[x\cdot(y+z)=(x\cdot y)+(x\cdot z),\qquad (x+y)\cdot z=(x\cdot z)+(y\cdot z),\qquad x\cdot1=x,\qquad1\cdot x=x.\] Is general first-order \(E\)-unification decidable? Namely, does one deterministic Turing machine halt on every finite signature and finite list of equations \(s_i\doteq t_i\), under the conventions below, and return YES exactly when a single finite-term substitution \(\sigma\) satisfies \(s_i\sigma=_E t_i\sigma\) for every \(i\)?
why: Distributivity couples two operations, so the standard decomposition methods for disjoint equational theories do not immediately apply. The multiplicative unit creates additional identifications between expanded and unexpanded expressions. Determining decidability for exactly this small axiom set would clarify a longstanding boundary in symbolic constraint solving, between known distributive fragments and stronger theories with undecidable unification.
status_note: The 2001 handbook explicitly lists this question as open. Checked the exact axiom sets in the two distinct 1996 positive results, the 1987 associative-extension negative result and the 2010 one-sided algorithm correction. A bounded primary-source search on 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the general four-identity target. Because no recent explicit status confirmation was found, scientific status remains uncertain.

importance.reason: A compact and longstanding equational-unification boundary, situated between decidable distributive fragments and undecidable associative extensions, with relevance to symbolic reasoning and theory combination.

sentences: Unification asks whether a common substitution can make every pair of supplied expressions equal under specified algebraic identities.
Here the identities are both distributive laws together with a two-sided multiplicative unit.
The expressions may also use uninterpreted symbols, and neither operation is assumed associative or commutative.
Known algorithms handle neighboring fragments, while undecidability results with additional associativity do not settle this exact theory.
A resolution would identify a longstanding boundary for symbolic equality reasoning under interacting algebraic laws.

definitions:
The fixed theory signature consists of binary symbols \(+\) and \(\cdot\) and a constant \(1\). An input signature \(F\) is any finite extension by uninterpreted function symbols of specified finite arities, including extra constants; these free symbols have no further equations. This uses the handbook's general-unification convention from §3.1 and §3.2.2 and includes elementary problems and problems with free constants as subcases. A term is a finite ordered rooted tree: a leaf is a variable or a constant, and a node labelled by a symbol of arity \(r\) has exactly \(r\) children. Variables come from a countable set of identifiers; only finitely many occur in an input. The equations form an explicitly written finite list, possibly empty. Signature declarations, arities, identifiers and complete term trees have finite binary encodings; no succinct circuits or infinite rational trees are inputs. A substitution assigns finite terms over \(F\) and variables to the finitely many input variables, fixes the other variables, and extends homomorphically through each function symbol. The same substitution applies to every equation. It is an ordinary simultaneous substitution, not an instruction to unfold terms indefinitely. Additional variables in its range are allowed. A unifier need not be most general, and the decision machine need not output one.

The relation \(=_E\) is the least equivalence relation on terms closed under application of every function symbol and substitutions, and containing every instance of the four displayed identities. Equivalently, equality has a finite equational derivation from exactly these identities, using reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, congruence and substitution. Parentheses and operand order therefore remain meaningful except where those identities identify them. Neither operation is assumed associative or commutative; no idempotence, additive zero, annihilation, additive inverse or cancellation law is included. The unit is two-sided and belongs to multiplication only. The notation resembles arithmetic, but the target is equality in the presented equational theory, not equality under a chosen integer or semiring interpretation. The same uniform machine must handle every finite input signature, variable count and equation list, halt on both YES and NO inputs, and use no oracle or random error. No time or memory bound is imposed, and no numerical tolerance applies.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that this precisely defined general-unification language is computable, or that it is not. A positive proof must represent finite signatures, terms, substitutions and the generated equational congruence, prove termination of one uniform algorithm on every well-formed input, and show that its YES output is equivalent to existence of a common unifier. A negative proof must establish noncomputability using only the four identities and the permitted free symbols. A result for a different axiom set, a matching problem with variables on only one side, or a nonterminating search for unifiers does not settle the card. The Lean proof must justify the exact signature convention it uses; a constants-only procedure does not automatically prove the general result. This source review is not a completed formal proof.

source_formulation.text: Is unification modulo both distributive laws and a two-sided multiplicative unit decidable?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the handbook question; general finite-signature unification convention stated explicitly

context_blocks.text: The handbook defines the two distributive theories separately, their union D, and the two-sided unit theory U. It then explicitly leaves D combined with U open. This is not an ordinary semiring problem because the associative, commutative and zero axioms of a semiring are absent.

Schmidt-Schauß’s 1996 distributive-unification theorem concerns the two distributive identities without the unit. Its publisher abstract lists those identities explicitly. The mention of unit-bearing auxiliary theories in that algorithm must not be mistaken for a multiplicative-unit axiom in its input theory.

A different 1996 result handles one-sided distributivity with a multiplicative unit. Having an algorithm after omitting either the second distributive law or the unit does not decide their combination.

Adding associativity of addition changes the situation: Tidén and Arnborg obtain undecidability for a theory with one-sided distributivity, associativity of addition and a one-sided multiplicative unit. That theorem does not settle the four-identity target, which lacks associativity.

The handbook separately distinguishes elementary unification, unification with extra constants and general unification with arbitrary free function symbols. The present card keeps the general first-order setting rather than silently restricting the problem to closed arithmetic-shaped terms.

The 2001 discussion repeats an early polynomial-time claim for the original one-sided algorithm. Narendran, Marshall and Mahapatra later give inputs requiring exponentially many steps for that algorithm. This correction concerns a neighboring algorithm’s running time, not a resolution of two-sided unification with a unit.

The September 2026 search checked these primary statements and later work indexed under distributivity and unification, without verifying a resolution of this exact theory. The old open statement is retained as historical evidence; its age and search absence are not proof of current openness.
